items.label: f02-csv-defuse
items.front: How does the CSV export stop formula injection?
items.back: A cell starting with = + - @ (plus tab or carriage return) is prefixed with a single quote, so a spreadsheet treats it as text.

items.label: f03-import-idempotent
items.front: What makes bulk import safe to resend?
items.back: Rows match existing issues by ExternalId (then by identifier like ENG-42), backed by a filtered unique index on (TeamId, ExternalId); import is all-or-nothing, and a dry run builds the exact plan a real import applies.

items.label: f04-outbox-limits
items.front: Known limits of the webhook outbox?
items.back: At-least-once, so consumers dedupe on the activity id; single instance only (the claim is not atomic); sequential sends give head-of-line blocking (up to 20 x 10 s per batch).

items.label: f01-status-codes
items.back: 401 no/unknown/revoked key; 403 right key but wrong role, or a row not yours to edit; 404 does not exist OR belongs to a team you are not on; 400 a well-formed request pointing at another team's reference (state, label, project, parent).

items.prompt: Why is recording an explicit call in each controller and not a SaveChanges interceptor?

choices.text: Interceptors run after commit, too late to join the transaction
An explicit call cannot be forgotten, unlike a global interceptor
An interceptor sees columns, not intent, and needs ambient state to name the actor
EF Core interceptors are unavailable on SQLite database connections

choices: Interceptors run after commit, too late to join the transaction
An explicit call cannot be forgotten, unlike a global interceptor
An interceptor sees columns, not intent, and needs ambient state to name the actor
EF Core interceptors are unavailable on SQLite database connections

items.explanation: The ADR: an interceptor cannot tell a re-parent from an assignment, cannot name the actor without ambient request state, and would report a rank rebalance as phantom edits. The cost of the explicit call is that it CAN be forgotten; tests catch that.

items.prompt: Issue A already "relates to" B. A request now creates "B relates to A". What is the outcome?

choices.text: 201, since Relates is symmetric and its duplicates are allowed
201, with the mirror stored as a second row in the other order
409, because Canonicalize orders the two ids into the same row
400, as a Relates link may be created only from the lower id

choices: 201, since Relates is symmetric and its duplicates are allowed
201, with the mirror stored as a second row in the other order
409, because Canonicalize orders the two ids into the same row
400, as a Relates link may be created only from the lower id

items.explanation: Relates endpoints are put in a fixed, stable order before the duplicate check, so the mirror spelling becomes the same (source, target, type) tuple; the unique index backs the clean 409.

items.prompt: Why is the timestamp put inside the HMAC input, as {timestamp}.{payload}, and not just sent beside it?

choices.text: It lets the signing secret be stored as a SHA-256 hash, like API keys
An attacker then cannot refresh it to make an old capture look current
It makes every payload unique, so consumers need no id to dedupe
Receivers can then skip the constant-time comparison of the two signatures

choices: It lets the signing secret be stored as a SHA-256 hash, like API keys
An attacker then cannot refresh it to make an old capture look current
It makes every payload unique, so consumers need no id to dedupe
Receivers can then skip the constant-time comparison of the two signatures

items.explanation: A body-only signature is valid forever; with the timestamp signed, a receiver rejects anything outside its tolerance and a replay cannot be refreshed. The secret is stored in the clear because it must sign.

items.prompt: A subscriber answers HTTP 429. How does WebhookRetryPolicy.Classify treat it?

choices.text: Permanent: every 4xx is a refusal that will not change later
None: any response with a status code counts as delivered
Permanent: any 4xx means the payload signature was rejected
Transient: rate limiting asks the sender to come back

choices: Permanent: every 4xx is a refusal that will not change later
None: any response with a status code counts as delivered
Permanent: any 4xx means the payload signature was rejected
Transient: rate limiting asks the sender to come back

items.explanation: The 429 arm sits before the >= 400 and < 500 Permanent arm; 408, 5xx and no response are also Transient, other 4xx and 3xx are Permanent.

items.prompt: Which id is sent as the webhook payload's `id`, and why that one?

choices.text: The activity id, which stays stable across retries and subscribers
The delivery id, so that each subscriber can dedupe its own copy
The issue id, because consumers track issues rather than single events
A fresh GUID for every attempt, so that retries can be told apart

choices: The activity id, which stays stable across retries and subscribers
The delivery id, so that each subscriber can dedupe its own copy
The issue id, because consumers track issues rather than single events
A fresh GUID for every attempt, so that retries can be told apart

items.explanation: Deliveries are at-least-once, so consumers dedupe on the activity id; the delivery id stays out of the body so one rendered, signed payload serves every subscriber.

items.prompt: Cycle 2 starts at exactly the instant cycle 1 ends. What does CycleSchedule.Overlaps return?

choices.text: false, since touching half-open intervals have zero common instants
true, since both cycles contain the boundary instant
true, until the two cycles' status fields are recomputed
true, unless a one-tick gap is left between the two cycles

choices: false, since touching half-open intervals have zero common instants
true, since both cycles contain the boundary instant
true, until the two cycles' status fields are recomputed
true, unless a one-tick gap is left between the two cycles

items.explanation: Cycles are [startsAt, endsAt): the end instant belongs to the next cycle. Overlaps is firstStart < secondEnd && secondStart < firstEnd, false for touching intervals. Status is derived, never stored.

items.prompt: A caller presents a revoked API key. How does the handler's answer compare with an unknown key?

choices.text: It returns the same "Invalid API key." failure as for an unknown key
It returns NoResult, letting the endpoint decide if a key was needed
It answers 403, since the key is genuine but no longer has a role
It returns a distinct "Key revoked" failure so the user can rotate

choices: It returns the same "Invalid API key." failure as for an unknown key
It returns NoResult, letting the endpoint decide if a key was needed
It answers 403, since the key is genuine but no longer has a role
It returns a distinct "Key revoked" failure so the user can rotate

items.explanation: Lines 59-65: one message for "no such key" and "revoked key", because telling them apart confirms a stolen token is genuine. NoResult is only for a request with no header at all.

items.prompt: A card is dropped between neighbours at Position 2.0 and 3.0, with plenty of gap. What gets written?

choices.text: Every card from 3.0 upward shifts by 1.0 to make room for it
It takes Position 2.0 and its old neighbour moves up to 3.0
Its Position becomes 2.5, and no other row in the column changes
The whole column is renumbered into 1.0 steps before the move

choices: Every card from 3.0 upward shifts by 1.0 to make room for it
It takes Position 2.0 and its old neighbour moves up to 3.0
Its Position becomes 2.5, and no other row in the column changes
The whole column is renumbered into 1.0 steps before the move

items.explanation: IssueRanker.Between returns l + (u - l) / 2, a one-row write. Renumbering (RankAt) only happens when NeedsRebalance finds the neighbours closer than MinGap = 1e-6.

items.prompt: Why does tracer-net hash API keys with SHA-256 and not with bcrypt or argon2?

choices.text: bcrypt cannot be run inside an ASP.NET Core authentication handler
A 192-bit random token has no keyspace for a slow hash to protect
SHA-256 can be reversed, so a lost token can be recovered later on
The tokens are chosen by users, and SHA-256 suits short secrets

choices: bcrypt cannot be run inside an ASP.NET Core authentication handler
A 192-bit random token has no keyspace for a slow hash to protect
SHA-256 can be reversed, so a lost token can be recovered later on
The tokens are chosen by users, and SHA-256 suits short secrets

items.explanation: A slow hash defends low-entropy, human-chosen secrets. A CSPRNG token of 24 bytes has nothing to brute-force, and a work factor would cost an expensive hash on every request.

choices.text: It checks permission first, so each foreign user id gets the same 403
The first route is admin-only, and the second is open to every member
Key ids are random, so a 403 on the second route could reveal nothing
User ids are public, while API key ids are kept secret by the design

choices: It checks permission first, so each foreign user id gets the same 403
The first route is admin-only, and the second is open to every member
Key ids are random, so a 403 on the second route could reveal nothing
User ids are public, while API key ids are kept secret by the design

items.explanation: A member gets the same 403 for any user id but their own, so nothing leaks; on /api-keys/{id} a 403 would only be reachable for a key that exists, an existence oracle for opaque ids.

items.prompt: ActivityRecorder.RecordAsync adds rows but never calls SaveChanges. What does that buy?

choices.text: Notifications are written later by a SaveChanges interceptor instead
Webhooks are sent before the change commits, then retried if it fails
Each Activity is saved first, so that the audit entry survives a rollback
The change, its Activity, webhook rows and notifications commit as one

choices: Notifications are written later by a SaveChanges interceptor instead
Webhooks are sent before the change commits, then retried if it fails
Each Activity is saved first, so that the audit entry survives a rollback
The change, its Activity, webhook rows and notifications commit as one

items.explanation: The recorder adds to the caller's DbContext, so the record, the outbox rows and the notifications join the mutation's transaction: all commit or none do.

items.prompt: The worker sends 5 deliveries from a batch, then the process dies before SaveChangesAsync. What happens after restart?

choices.text: None is resent, since each send marked its own row as delivered
All 5 go out again, as their results died with the process
Only the fifth is resent, since every other attempt saved alone
The batch is dead-lettered and waits for a manual retry instead

choices: None is resent, since each send marked its own row as delivered
All 5 go out again, as their results died with the process
Only the fifth is resent, since every other attempt saved alone
The batch is dead-lettered and waits for a manual retry instead

items.explanation: Attempt results are saved once per batch (WebhookSender.cs:49-52); a crash before that save leaves the rows Pending and due, so they are re-sent: within at-least-once, with a whole-batch duplicate window.

items.prompt: A non-admin member who belongs only to team A calls GET /api/teams/{teamB}/issues. Which status comes back?

choices.text: 400, as team B is a real reference not the caller's
401, since the API key is valid only inside team A
403, because team B exists and the caller is not on it
404, exactly the answer a made-up team id would get

choices: 400, as team B is a real reference not the caller's
401, since the API key is valid only inside team A
403, because team B exists and the caller is not on it
404, exactly the answer a made-up team id would get

items.explanation: ADR 0002 collapses existence and permission: a team you are not on is reported like a team that never existed, so probing ids cannot map the workspace. 400 is for pointing at another team's reference from inside your own request.
